chapter_theme: The elder's sermon to the young prince Asodharan, with caged birds, karma that follows like a thread and the dread of rebirth, ends in the prince's freeing of a cygnet, his father's order to rule first, his argument that kin are strangers and his leaving with his wives; the chapter then returns to the king hearing the great ascetic, the Charanas' departure and the grief of the women at his announced renunciation.

cast.role: the unnamed elder who preaches to the prince
the young prince of Bhumi Tilakam who renounces
the prince's father, the king of kings
the prince's wives who also take the vow
the hero, now an old king, who hears the great ascetic
the great ascetic who preaches to the king
the sky-going ascetics who rise away
the king's women who weep at his vow

2874.reading: The speaker says that people ruled by desire, anger and greed, those who deck themselves with garlands and sandal, and those who eat only from hunger are not a refuge, and bids the hearer bow to no feet but those of the lord who has none of these.
2874.nuance: The speaker is not named; the verse follows a sermon that begins at 2867 and is taken here as the same voice. வாமன் is read as a title of the passionless lord, not a name.
2874.event: The elder tells the prince to worship only the lord free of passion.

claims.claim: only the lord free of desire, anger and greed is worth worshipping, not those who are ruled by them

2875.reading: Parrots, mynas, peacocks, swans and many other birds cry out when they are torn from their kin and shut under guard; the speaker tells the renowned prince that those who do this will themselves be parted from their kin, and that the keeping of them is unseemly.
2875.nuance: This answers the scene at 2864, where the birds are found taken from the pond. The verse says the captors will leave their kin; it does not say when or by what mechanism.
2875.event: The elder rebukes the prince for keeping caged birds away from their flocks.

claims.claim: those who tear creatures from their kin and cage them will themselves be parted from their kin

2876.reading: As the thread in a lotus stalk does not break when the stalk is torn, so the deed of earlier lives does not leave when the body leaves: it clings to the soul, enters whatever body it enters, follows behind and burns it with the fierce fire of endless suffering.
2876.nuance: The thread image makes karma a continuous strand that outlasts each body; the verse names no way to cut it, so its remedy has to come from the verses that follow.

claims.claim: evil deeds cling to the soul through every change of body and burn it with suffering

2877.reading: If one turns the mind to kindness toward living souls, the old deed plays with the soul as a bird plays with its own shadow, and without a lapse yields from the mind whatever one desires, as a cow gives milk to the milker.
2877.nuance: The cow and the bird with its shadow are the two comparisons; the syntax of lines 2-4 is hard and the comparison of the second is read loosely.

claims.claim: kindness to living souls makes the old deed yield what one desires

2878.reading: A tortoise set on a jewelled post in deep water thinks of its mate in the blue lily bed, and so women with keen fish-like eyes who dwell on desire and wealth lose their lives, being small in understanding.
2878.nuance: The grammar of lines 3-4 is hard, so who is said to give up life (the women, or the men who think of them) is not fixed; the simile is read as one of longing that does not release.

claims.claim: those who dwell on desire and wealth lose their lives through small understanding

2879.reading: When Death, who ruins all splendour, catches a man in his diamond net, the wise leave garlanded women and wealth and think only of dharma, which shows itself like a river coming down a mountain, and so climb a golden way to rule the two heavens.

claims.claim: at death wealth and wives are left and only dharma remains to carry one to heaven

2880.reading: Having listened to dharma, the prince melts like cloth touched by fire, lets the female cygnet he had taken go free in the pool, and then does something with the gathering of its kin that the last word leaves unclear.
2880.nuance: The last word வித்தினான் ('sowed') is read here as bringing the flock together again; the verse does not say so.
2880.event: Asodharan releases the cygnet he had captured into the pond and rejoins it to its flock.

2881.reading: Like effort to cure an old wound, the prince casts out matching desire with disgust, fearing that this is sin and dreading the disease of birth, and is like one holding nectar in his mouth.
2881.nuance: The last line's comparison to nectar in the mouths of dark-eyed women is hard to place and may refer to the prince's earlier pleasure.
2881.event: Asodharan gives up desire out of fear of sin and rebirth.

claims.claim: desire is a sin and birth a disease from which one must be healed by giving it up

2882.reading: Like a spotted elephant sprung on by a lion, the bowman cries aloud that he has tasted desire's poison day after day, and will leave the golden-armed women and do pure tapas, lord.
2882.nuance: The speaker is read as the prince and the addressee அடிகள் as his father, since the next verse has a king answer the youth.
2882.event: Asodharan cries out that he will give up the women and do tapas.

claims.claim: desire is a poison that one has been eating, and tapas is its cure

2883.reading: Hearing the youth, the chariot-king answers that he should first take his bright-crowned share, guard the kingdom bounded by the roaring sea, give all to a worthy son and only then renounce.
2883.nuance: Whether the chariot-king is the father is not said; the verse answers a youth's vow with the order of duties, and the story that follows does not wait for a son.
2883.event: The king tells the prince to rule and pass on the kingdom before he renounces.

claims.claim: a king should rule and hand on his kingdom to a son before renouncing

2884.reading: Like a man who has escaped the prison of killing and is run down, seized and thrust into a hard cell again, he asks whether these kin he cannot shake off are kin or enemies, and is like one who throws a priceless gem into mid-ocean.
2884.nuance: The question is in the youth's mouth and the gem comparison may be the narrator's; the next verse gives his answer.

claims.claim: kin who bind one to the world are enemies rather than kin

2885.reading: He reasons that those about him are not his own, since in past births they were strangers and in the bodies to come they will be strangers again, so there is no kin; and the garlanded one cuts the bond of affection through.
2885.event: Asodharan reasons that no one is truly kin and cuts the bonds of affection.

claims.claim: no one is kin across births, since all were strangers before and will be strangers again

2886.reading: As a jointed doll made by a master falls apart in every joint when its pins are loosed, so every sense fails when the joint of speech fails; the prince leaves the delight of the senses and goes surrounded by two thousand.
2886.nuance: The doll image describes the body's failing as a mechanism; the verse then turns to the prince's leaving without saying that his leaving is this failing.
2886.event: Asodharan leaves his pleasures and goes out with two thousand companions.

claims.claim: the body is a jointed contrivance whose senses all fail together when one joint gives way

2887.reading: As the flesh-smelling monitor lizard that clings to its hole when a plank is torn away can be moved by some means, so on the cause of a single word the garlanded prince left the women with arrow-bright eyes and became a holy man.
2887.nuance: கடவுளானான் is read as 'became a holy one', one who has taken the vow, not as becoming a deity. The details of the lizard simile are not fully clear.
2887.event: Asodharan abandons the women and becomes an ascetic after one word.

claims.claim: the firmest clinging to the world can be broken by a single word

2888.reading: The prince and the women with shining bangles and garlanded hair, fearing the dreaded four states of birth, took the summit of fine tapas.
2888.nuance: நாற்கதி is the four courses of rebirth (hell, beast, human, god) of Jain teaching; the verse does not list them.
2888.event: Asodharan and his wives take the vow of tapas.

claims.claim: the four states of birth are to be feared and escaped by tapas

2889.reading: A speaker greets one who by tapas done in regard for conduct and shame became a bright god, lord of the Kalpa-dwellers called Sasaran, and has come ruling a jewelled sky-world.
2889.nuance: Neither speaker nor addressee is named; the addressee may be Civakan, whose earlier birth the sermon tells, or the prince now a god. The last line is hard.

claims.claim: tapas done with regard for conduct and shame earns lordship of heaven

2890.reading: The speaker tells the garlanded king that in earlier days he parted others and so seems to have been shut in a prison himself, and the speaker's words are medicine for the disease of woeful births.
2890.nuance: This returns to the cage of 2875 and puts the repayment in the same form; who is addressed is not fixed.

claims.claim: one who cages and parts others is in turn caged and parted

2891.reading: At the words of the great ascetic, mountain-like and full of a sinless sermon, the king with the poison-spitting spear sits in fear and trembles as though an arrow had fallen.
2891.nuance: The king is read as Civakan; the verse names neither. The sermon's content is not given here.
2891.event: The king trembles at the ascetic's sermon.

2892.reading: The king, ringed by peacock-like women, bows his jewelled crown and praises the glorious feet of the ascetics.
2892.event: The king bows his crown at the ascetics' feet and praises them.

2893.reading: The Charanas, high in great tapas, rise like the sun and moon, and the sky grows bright as they go.
2893.nuance: The Charanas are the sky-going ascetics of Jain tradition; the verse reports their rising and does not teach how it is done.
2893.event: The Charanas ascend through the sky.

claims.claim: ascetics of great tapas travel the sky

2894.reading: When the Charanas have gone, the eyes of the vine-slender women with sandal-pasted breasts, bright as spears, brim over like blue lilies filled with water.
2894.event: The women weep after the Charanas leave.

2895.reading: The king, his chest bright with southern sandal like a golden mountain under the moon, gives the slender women no kind word and goes to the banner-hung palace.
2895.event: The king leaves the women without a word and goes to the palace.

2896.reading: On a soft cotton couch the women with sea-wide hips lie with their cloud-dark moon faces dimmed, their beauty withered by sighs of poison.
2896.event: The women lie wasting on their couch.

2897.reading: The women, who thin like what the white-fanged snake has eaten and leaves, who can say nothing but one thing like the cloud-bird, lose their golden pallor and the colour of their bright gems.
2897.nuance: The two comparisons (the snake's leavings and the bird of the cloud) are hard to place; the sense of loss is clear but the figure is not.
2897.event: The women lose their colour and ornament in grief.

2898.reading: The women with parrot-sweet speech, their anklets crying out, weep and toss like carp in water, because the king in his garland and ring has told them of his renunciation.
2898.nuance: The verse says only that he spoke of renunciation; his words are not given.
2898.event: The women weep because the king has told them he will renounce.

links.note: 2875 sets caged birds crying for their kin and warns the captors that they will be parted from theirs; Naladiyar 122 says those who cage partridges and quails will go as slaves to strangers in irons.
links.teaches: Together they show the same crime repaid in two forms, loss of kin and loss of freedom, which neither names alone.

gains.a: the verse's warning of parting from kin gains a second, bodily form of repayment, irons and service under strangers
gains.b: the quatrain's repayment for caging gains the grief of the caged, the birds' separation from their flock, that its sentence mirrors

links.note: 2875 warns that those who cage birds will be parted from their kin; in 2880 the prince who heard the dharma sets the captured cygnet free in the pool.
links.teaches: The warning and the release show a sermon changing a deed within a few verses, which a rule on its own does not.

links.note: 2876 says the deed clings to the soul like a thread in a lotus stalk and follows it into each body; Naladiyar 120 says nothing goes with a person but the deeds done.
links.teaches: One gives the thread image of how a deed follows, the other the fact that only deeds follow, so each answers what the other leaves open.

gains.a: the verse's following deed gains the plain statement that it is the only thing that goes with the person, body and wealth being left
gains.b: the quatrain's 'what goes with a person' gains a picture of how it goes: an unbroken thread that burns as it follows

links.note: 2876 gives the old deed as a thread that cannot be torn away and burns the soul; Tirumanthiram 117 says the malas burn like cotton only when the sunstone meets the sun's presence, and not before.
links.teaches: The Jain verse leaves the deed unbroken and the Saiva verse says what ends it, so the Saiva verse limits the Jain one's permanence.

gains.a: the thread that follows through every body is shown to have, in a Saiva view, an end at the coming of grace
gains.b: the malas that grace burns gain a rival account in which the burden is a clinging deed that no god is said to remove

links.note: 2883 has the father tell the youth who wants to renounce to rule and pass on the kingdom first; Kural 342 says to renounce while there is time.
links.teaches: The Kural leaves open what counts as time, and the father fixes it as the time after the duties of a king are done.

gains.a: the father's delay gains the Kural's urgency, which makes his 'first rule' a hard answer and not a mild one
gains.b: the Kural's 'while there is time' gains a worked limit, the discharge of a kingdom's duties, that its bare phrase does not give

links.note: 2883 tells the youth to rule first and give the kingdom to a son before renouncing; Naladiyar 11 says the wise renounced in childhood, knowing grey hair will come.
links.teaches: One praises renouncing at the earliest, the other puts duty before the vow, so they mark two views of when the right time begins.

gains.a: the father's order of duties gains the opposing view that foresight, not age, marks the wise and that waiting is the fool's course
gains.b: the quatrain's praise of early renunciation gains a king's reason for delay, the kingdom that must be handed on

links.note: 2884 asks whether the kin he cannot be rid of are kin or enemies; 2885 answers that they are neither, being strangers in past births and in those to come.
links.teaches: The answer is a rebirth argument and not a complaint, so the question of kin turns on how many lives one counts.

links.note: 2885 says kin were strangers in past births and will be strangers in births to come; Naladiyar 30 says kin come unasked and go wordlessly, leaving the body like a bird its nesting tree.
links.teaches: The quatrain holds within one life and the verse extends the same estrangement across births, which turns a sad fact into a ground for cutting the bond.

gains.a: the verse's no-kin argument gains the plain picture of kin arriving and leaving unasked in a single life
gains.b: the quatrain's passing kin gain a reach into past and future births, and with it a reason to cut the tie

links.note: 2885 has the prince reason that there is no kin and cut the bond of love; Siddhar 55 wishes to put kin away, like a lotus leaf on water, with the mind far off.
links.teaches: The Siddhar states a wish for detachment and the prince acts on an argument, so together they show the wish and its grounds.

gains.a: the prince's cut gains the Siddhar's image of being among kin without being wetted by them
gains.b: the Siddhar's wish to put kin away gains the argument that kin were strangers across births, which the song never gives

links.note: 2886 compares the body to a doll that falls apart joint by joint when its pins are loosed; Siddhar 42 asks when the puppet taken up to match the two karmas will be thrown down.
links.teaches: The epic shows the doll's falling as a mechanism and the Siddhar wants to throw it down, so one explains how the body fails and the other why it is to be cast off.

gains.a: the doll's failing joints gain the Siddhar's reason for the body, a payment for two deeds, to be thrown down
gains.b: the Siddhar's puppet gains an account of how it comes apart, each pin loosing the rest

links.note: 2887 shows a clinging that holds like the monitor's grip broken by a single word; Kural 350 says to cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go.
links.teaches: The Kural names the means as a right object of clinging and the verse names a single word, so the means can be a sentence from a teacher.

gains.a: the single word that broke the prince's clinging gains the Kural's account of why a word can work: it points to the unclinging one
gains.b: the Kural's command to cling in order to let go gains a case where one saying did it

source_issues: Verses 2876, 2878-2884, 2886-2888, 2897 and 2898 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.

The speakers of 2874-2879 and 2889-2890 are not named; 'elder' is a working id. Whether 2889-2890 address the prince now a god or Civakan hearing his earlier birth, and whether 2891 onward is Civakan, is inferred from the story and not fixed by the Tamil.
2877, 2878, 2881, 2887 and 2897 have similes whose syntax is hard to parse; their readings are marked uncertain.
